title: Why a finite-speed quotient is not the mass decrease
spoken: The finite-speed proxy is defined as twice the exact kinetic-energy drop divided by v squared.
explanation: This definition is useful for approaching the low-speed coefficient. At finite speed the proxy is generally larger than L/c². At v = 0 the quotient is not applicable; the analytic limit must be evaluated separately.
assumptions: Two equal, opposite light pulses remove total positive energy L; their symmetry removes recoil in the body’s rest frame.
The two inertial descriptions refer to the same emission and the same body boundary; |v| < c.
These are authored modern teaching equations, not a transcription or printed-notation concordance.
The relation H − E = K + C uses the same unknown additive C before and after emission. This is a premise; conservation and subtraction do not prove it.
v is nonzero for this quotient; no zero-over-zero value is supplied.

notes.title: A finite-speed proxy, not the mass loss
notes.explanation: This is 2ΔK/v² evaluated at a nonzero speed. Its speed dependence is exactly why the low-speed limit is needed. At v = 0 this quotient is not applicable, not zero.

notes.title: Positive kinetic-energy drop
notes.explanation: ΔK means K₀ − K₁ in this card: before minus after. It is identified from the ledger subtraction only under the unchanged-offset premise.

notes.title: Multiply the factors
notes.explanation: Twice the exact kinetic-energy drop is the numerator, not twice the quadratic approximation.

notes.title: Same observer speed
notes.explanation: v is the signed relative speed between inertial descriptions. Its magnitude is less than c. It is held fixed while the body emits.

notes.title: Square the dimensional speed
notes.explanation: v² carries square metres per square second. Energy divided by v² therefore has units of mass.

notes.title: Compare with the Newtonian coefficient
notes.explanation: Divide by one half v² to inspect the coefficient a Newtonian kinetic-energy form would have. Taking this ratio at finite speed is not taking its limit.
